4.1 Measuring Return and Risk

Two average returns

Section titled “Two average returns”

An investment returned R1,…,RnR_1, \ldots, R_nR1​,…,Rn​ over the past nnn years (simple return). There are two ways to compute an “average return”.

The arithmetic mean return is the simple average of the yearly returns:

Rˉ=1n∑t=1nRt\bar R = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} R_tRˉ=n1​t=1∑n​Rt​

The geometric mean return is the yearly rate that, compounded, gives the same final wealth; it is also called the compound annual growth rate:

G=[(1+R1)(1+R2)⋯(1+Rn)]1/n−1G = \left[(1 + R_1)(1 + R_2) \cdots (1 + R_n)\right]^{1/n} - 1G=[(1+R1​)(1+R2​)⋯(1+Rn​)]1/n−1

For example, a fund rises 25% in the first year and falls 20% in the second. The arithmetic mean is 2.5%, but 1.25×0.8=11.25 \times 0.8 = 11.25×0.8=1: after two years wealth has not changed, so the geometric mean is 0.

The two answer different questions:

  • The arithmetic mean estimates the expected return for next year (expected value). If each year’s return comes from the same distribution, it is an unbiased estimate of the expected return.
  • The geometric mean describes the growth the holder actually got over the period. In terms of the log return, ln⁡(1+G)\ln(1 + G)ln(1+G) is exactly the average of the yearly log returns.

Unless all yearly returns are equal, the geometric mean is below the arithmetic mean. In 0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference, median wealth was below mean wealth; that is the other side of the same fact: long-run median wealth grows roughly at the geometric mean, while mean wealth grows at the arithmetic mean.

Check C1
A fund returned +30% and −20% over the past two years. Which statement is correct?
5% is the arithmetic mean. What investors actually earned depends on how many times their wealth was multiplied over the two years.
Returns compound; they do not add. Work out 1.3×0.81.3 \times 0.81.3×0.8.
Think: when returns go up and down, which is higher, compound growth or the simple average?

Volatility drag

Section titled “Volatility drag”

How far below the arithmetic mean is the geometric mean? Let each year’s return have expected value μ\muμ and standard deviation σ\sigmaσ. One can show (Exercises Question 1) that

G≈μ−σ22G \approx \mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}G≈μ−2σ2​

Volatility pushes the compound growth rate below the arithmetic mean; this is volatility drag. For example, with μ=10%\mu = 10\%μ=10% and σ=20%\sigma = 20\%σ=20%, G≈10%−(20%)22=8%G \approx 10\% - \frac{(20\%)^2}{2} = 8\%G≈10%−2(20%)2​=8%.

Check C2
Funds A and B both have an arithmetic mean return of 10% a year. A's volatility is 10% and B's is 30%. Held for the long run, roughly how much lower is B's compound growth rate than A's?
Compound growth depends not only on the arithmetic mean but also on how volatile the returns are.
20 points is the difference in volatilities. Is the drag proportional to volatility itself?
Knowing the expected return and the standard deviation is enough to approximate the compound growth rate.

Leverage makes the issue sharper. Let the risk-free rate be rrr. An investor puts LLL times his wealth into a risky asset with expected return μ\muμ and volatility σ\sigmaσ, borrowing the rest at rrr (when L<1L < 1L<1, lending the rest at rrr). The portfolio’s expected return and volatility are

μL=r+L(μ−r),σL=Lσ\mu_L = r + L(\mu - r), \qquad \sigma_L = L\sigmaμL​=r+L(μ−r),σL​=Lσ

The expected return rises in a straight line with LLL, but the volatility drag σL22\frac{\sigma_L^2}{2}2σL2​​ grows with the square of LLL. Does more leverage always raise long-run growth? Figure 2-1 plots the two lines.

Check C3
In Figure 2-1, the risky asset has an expected return of 9% and a volatility of 18%. As leverage rises step by step from 1 to 4, the portfolio's compound growth rate:
The expected return rises in a straight line with leverage, but how fast does the drag grow? Look at the solid line at high leverage.
Just above a leverage of 1, look at whether the solid line goes up or down.
Are return and risk magnified at the same rate? The expected return is proportional to LLL; what about the drag?

Volatility and annualizing

Section titled “Volatility and annualizing”

The standard deviation of returns (standard deviation) is also called volatility. A standard deviation computed from monthly or daily returns must be converted to a yearly figure to be compared. If returns in different periods are independent, the variance of the sum of TTT periods’ returns is TTT times the variance of one period (0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance), so

σa=σm12\sigma_a = \sigma_m \sqrt{12}σa​=σm​12​

where σm\sigma_mσm​ is the standard deviation of monthly returns and σa\sigma_aσa​ that of yearly returns. This gives the annualized volatility. With daily returns, multiply by 252\sqrt{252}252​ (about 252 trading days a year). For example, a monthly volatility of 5% gives an annualized volatility of about 5%×12≈17.3%5\% \times \sqrt{12} \approx 17.3\%5%×12​≈17.3%.

This conversion relies on the assumption that periods are independent. In practice returns in different periods may be correlated, and then the converted figure is biased.

Check C4
If returns in neighboring months are positively correlated (rises tend to be followed by rises), multiplying monthly volatility by 12\sqrt{12}12​ understates the true yearly volatility.
Think: besides the sum of the monthly variances, what other terms are in the variance of the sum of 12 monthly returns? With positive correlation, are those terms positive or negative?

Maximum drawdown

Section titled “Maximum drawdown”

The standard deviation treats rises and falls alike, and does not show how long losses last. What investors feel more directly is how far wealth falls from a high point. The largest fall in wealth from a previous peak to a later trough over a period is the maximum drawdown.

Two large drawdowns in US stock market history: the S&P 500 index (excluding dividends) fell about 86% from September 1929 to June 1932, and about 57% from October 2007 to March 2009. The deeper the fall, the harder it is to get back to the earlier level, and the longer it takes (Check C5). For investors who must withdraw money regularly (such as retirees), selling assets during a deep drawdown turns paper losses into permanent ones, so drawdowns matter more to them than the standard deviation.

Check C5
A portfolio has fallen 50% from its peak. How much must it rise to get back to the peak?
The rise is measured on the amount after the fall. Does a 50% rise from 50 get back to 100?
To go from 50 back to 100, how much must be added? What percentage of 50 is that?
To go from 50 back to 100, how many times 50 must be added?

The Sharpe ratio

Section titled “The Sharpe ratio”

Comparing two investments requires looking at both return and risk. Let the risk-free rate be rfr_frf​. The Sharpe ratio is the excess return earned per unit of volatility:

S=Rˉ−rfσS = \frac{\bar R - r_f}{\sigma}S=σRˉ−rf​​

For example, a portfolio with an average return of 9%, a risk-free rate of 3% and a volatility of 15% has a Sharpe ratio of 9%−3%15%=0.4\frac{9\% - 3\%}{15\%} = 0.415%9%−3%​=0.4.

The Sharpe ratio measures risk by the standard deviation, so it shares its limits: fat tails (fat tails), large losses that occur only rarely, and returns “smoothed” because an asset trades infrequently can all make it overstate the quality of an investment (Exercises Question 3).

Check C6
Investing in a portfolio with 2 times leverage (borrowing at the risk-free rate) doubles the Sharpe ratio of the investment.
Think: with 2 times leverage, by what factor does the excess return μL−r\mu_L - rμL​−r change? And the volatility σL\sigma_LσL​? The Sharpe ratio is their ratio.

Historical data

Section titled “Historical data”

In data compiled by Damodaran (New York University), from 1928 to 2025 the S&P 500 (including dividends) had a geometric mean return of about 10.0% a year, 10-year US Treasury bonds about 4.5%, and 3-month Treasury bills about 3.4%. The standard deviation of yearly stock returns is about 20%, and the arithmetic mean is about 2 percentage points above the geometric mean, consistent with σ22\frac{\sigma^2}{2}2σ2​.

The amount by which the expected return on stocks exceeds the return on a riskless asset is the equity premium. By the figures above, stocks have historically earned about 6.6 percentage points a year more than Treasury bills. Two cautions apply when using this to estimate the future equity premium:

  • The estimation error is large. With a yearly standard deviation of about 20%, even nearly a century of data leaves a standard error (standard error) of about 2 percentage points on the average return (Exercises Question 4).
  • The US was one of the best-performing stock markets of the 20th century. Looking only at a market that turned out to be successful overstates the typical return on stocks.

4.11 Capital Market Assumptions discusses how to estimate future expected returns more systematically.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • The arithmetic mean Rˉ\bar RRˉ estimates next year’s expected return; the geometric mean GGG is the compound growth the holder actually got. With volatile returns, G<RˉG < \bar RG<Rˉ.
  • Volatility drag: G≈μ−σ22G \approx \mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}G≈μ−2σ2​. Leverage raises the expected return in a straight line and the volatility drag with the square.
  • With independent periods, annualized volatility is σa=σm12\sigma_a = \sigma_m \sqrt{12}σa​=σm​12​.
  • Maximum drawdown is the largest fall from a previous peak to a later trough; it shows risk that the standard deviation does not.
  • The Sharpe ratio S=Rˉ−rfσS = \frac{\bar R - r_f}{\sigma}S=σRˉ−rf​​ measures excess return per unit of volatility, but inherits the limits of the standard deviation.
  • From 1928 to 2025, US stocks returned about 10.0% a year (geometric) and Treasury bills about 3.4%; estimates of the historical equity premium have large errors.
